titles.name: Crown of England
titles.note: Gameplay realm root.
titles.description: The Crown of England unites a realm of royal lands, noble lordships, boroughs and liberties. Its authority extends across territories with differing local rights and customs. In 1471, the rival houses of Lancaster and York contest possession of the throne.

titles.name: Crown of Scotland

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: Gameplay realm root.
titles.description: The Scottish Crown presides over a realm of earldoms, lordships, royal burghs and other local jurisdictions. Noble estates and chartered towns retain distinct rights within the kingdom.

titles.name: Lordship of the Isles

titles.name: Honour of Pontefract
titles.note: The honour was a major Yorkshire component of the Duchy. This names the local estate rather than labelling all its land Lancaster. Richard of Gloucester's later 1471 stewardship is not applied to the early-spring snapshot.
titles.description: Honour of Pontefract is centred on Pontefract Castle. It is associated with West Riding of Yorkshire. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Honour of Lancaster
titles.note: The 1267 grant explicitly included honour, county, castle and town. Honour and palatine jurisdiction must remain distinct concepts; this does not make every Lancashire estate a Lancastrian demesne.
titles.description: Honour of Lancaster is centred on Lancaster. It is associated with Lancashire, county palatine. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Piel estate
titles.area: Furness, Lancashire north of the sands
titles.note: The abbot fortified his manor in 1327 and the castle remained an abbey possession until the Dissolution. This is an ecclesiastical territorial dependency, not evidence for the configured Stanley ownership. Do not change campaign ownership in this research pass.
titles.description: Piel estate is centred on Piel Castle. It is associated with Furness, Lancashire north of the sands. The estate's history is tied to the landed possessions of a religious house.

titles.name: Liverpool castle estate
titles.note: Scholarly accounts use Duchy records and distinguish the Molyneux hereditary constableship from ownership. Duchy parent is a supported estate association proposed for mapping; a precise 1471 tenure extract remains to be checked. The VCH web page returned 403 and is not presented as inspected evidence.
titles.description: Liverpool castle estate is centred on Liverpool Castle. It is associated with West Derby hundred, Lancashire. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Barony of Kendal
titles.note: Kendal was the caput of a territorial barony, subsequently divided into moieties. Use this local identity provisionally for the castle; the precise castle-bearing moiety and its 1471 superior tenure require verification. Neither Lancashire nor the Earl of Westmorland follows from location.
titles.description: Barony of Kendal is centred on Kendal Castle. It is associated with Southern Westmorland.

titles.name: City of Chester
titles.note: The earldom's palatine government operated at Chester. City jurisdiction and borough franchises require a separate charter audit before treating the town as demesne. This proposed territorial parent replaces an unsupported Lancaster/Rivers inference; it is not a finding of ownership.
titles.description: City of Chester is centred on Chester. It is associated with Cheshire palatinate.

titles.name: Beeston castle estate
titles.note: The castle was built by Ranulf, Earl of Chester, taken by the Crown in 1237, and granted with the earldom to the future Edward I in 1254. It remained a royal castle into the sixteenth century; a Vernon constable/owner configuration is separate from territorial identity.
titles.description: Beeston castle estate is centred on Beeston Castle. It is associated with Cheshire. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Lordship of Chirk
titles.note: Chirk is a Marcher castle and lordship, not a subdivision inferred from Cheshire. The National Trust establishes its Mortimer/FitzAlan history but does not settle the exact early-1471 superior tenure. No automatic palatinate or remote peerage parent is assigned.
titles.description: Lordship of Chirk is centred on Chirk Castle. It is associated with Chirkland, Welsh March. A Marcher lordship combines landed authority with the distinctive rights and customs of the Welsh March.

titles.name: Lordship of the High Peak
titles.note: English Heritage records the Peak estate's incorporation into the Duchy in 1372. The castle's historic local jurisdiction is the Peak, not Cheshire merely because of its configured parent.
titles.description: Lordship of the High Peak is centred on Peveril Castle. It is associated with Peak, Derbyshire.

titles.name: Earldom of Warwick
titles.note: The castle and Warwick inheritance belonged to Anne Beauchamp and Richard Neville before Barnet. Warwick and Salisbury are separate dignities and inheritances: do not manufacture a single geographical duchy of both. Immediate superior tenure is not established by this estate history.
titles.description: Earldom of Warwick is centred on Warwick Castle. It is associated with Warwickshire.

titles.name: City of Coventry
titles.area: Warwickshire; county of the city from 1451
titles.note: Coventry became a county corporate in 1451. Its prior's and earl's halves and the Cheylesmore estate are distinct interests; the whole borough cannot be assigned to Warwick's territorial earldom simply from a shared shire or patron. Exact local property partitions need a further charter/manorial audit.
titles.description: City of Coventry is centred on Coventry. It is associated with Warwickshire; county of the city from 1451. Its county status concerns the town's civic jurisdiction rather than a hereditary earldom.

titles.name: Kenilworth castle estate
titles.note: Kenilworth entered the Lancastrian inheritance through Edmund and John of Gaunt, then royal hands with Henry IV. Its location near Warwick does not subordinate it to the Earl of Warwick.
titles.description: Kenilworth castle estate is centred on Kenilworth Castle. It is associated with Warwickshire. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Northampton castle estate
titles.note: Official local histories identify the royal castle. Crown is a proposed direct parent grounded in that status, pending a 1471 grant/custody audit. Neither the Earl of Northampton nor Warwick's present configured umbrella proves ownership or mesne tenure.
titles.description: Northampton castle estate is centred on Northampton Castle. It is associated with Northamptonshire.

titles.name: Worcester castle estate
titles.note: Descriptive local estate is retained provisionally. Archaeology confirms the castle environs, but these sources do not establish its 1471 immediate tenure. The commonly reported royal status and hereditary Beauchamp constableship need documentary separation; do not infer a Sutton or Warwick parent. VCH access was blocked.
titles.description: Worcester castle estate is centred on Worcester Castle. It is associated with Worcestershire. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Borough of Newcastle upon Tyne
titles.note: The Tyne and Wear Archives description records the 1400 charter separating the borough from Northumberland, expressly excepting castle and precincts. Crown parent represents royal borough jurisdiction provisionally, not a new earldom. Newcastle is not Westmorland or County Durham.
titles.description: Borough of Newcastle upon Tyne is centred on Newcastle upon Tyne. It is associated with Northumberland; town county from 1400. Its county status concerns the town's civic jurisdiction rather than a hereditary earldom.

titles.name: Durham episcopal castle estate
titles.note: The castle was the bishop's residence and centre of palatine authority. It is not a Greystoke barony beneath Newcastle. Ecclesiastical correction is research only pending the church branch. Avoid projecting the later expression Prince-Bishopric into a 1471 title label.
titles.description: Durham episcopal castle estate is centred on Durham Castle. It is associated with County palatine of Durham. The estate's history is tied to the temporal lands of a bishopric.

titles.name: Lordship of Barnard Castle
titles.note: A distinct Balliol lordship subsequently held by the Earls of Warwick; Richard Neville was alive in early spring 1471. Estate ownership does not alone establish a feudal parent of Earldom of Warwick. Its contested relationship with Durham/Richmond needs separate legal evidence; Gloucester's post-Barnet acquisition is excluded.
titles.description: Lordship of Barnard Castle is centred on Barnard Castle. It is associated with Teesdale, Durham border.

titles.name: Lordship of Skelton
titles.note: The Brus partition and Fauconberg estate history identify the local lordship. This is Cleveland, not County Durham. The precise 1471 estate interest and superior tenure need verification; the configured Fitzhugh family is not evidence of either.
titles.description: Lordship of Skelton is centred on Skelton Castle. It is associated with Cleveland, North Riding of Yorkshire.

titles.name: City of Carlisle
titles.note: The official castle history establishes Carlisle's royal border stronghold and wardenship. It is contextual evidence, not a city charter or proof of the whole borough's tenure. Local city identity is proposed pending municipal evidence; no Clifford barony over Cumberland is inferred.
titles.description: City of Carlisle is centred on Carlisle. It is associated with Cumberland, West March.

titles.name: Lordship of Penrith
titles.note: The manor was granted to Ralph Neville in 1396 and Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, held it until Barnet. This establishes the estate identity and chronology, not an intervening Cumberland or Warwick territorial superiority. Richard of Gloucester's later acquisition is excluded.
titles.description: Lordship of Penrith is centred on Penrith Castle. It is associated with Cumberland.

titles.name: Lordship of Fotheringhay
titles.note: A local castle lordship and administrative centre for York's Midland estates. The York dynastic association is established; a feudal super-title of Duchy of York is not established by residence or office alone. This estate is not a territorial proxy for Yorkshire.
titles.description: Lordship of Fotheringhay is centred on Fotheringhay Castle. It is associated with Northamptonshire.

titles.name: City of York
titles.area: Yorkshire; county of the city from 1396
titles.note: The published translation of Richard II's 1396 charter from York City Archives establishes direct royal civic liberties and county status. This is a municipal jurisdiction, not a hereditary earldom subordinate to the Duchy of York. Surrounding Yorkshire is not automatically duchy demesne.
titles.description: City of York is centred on York. It is associated with Yorkshire; county of the city from 1396. Its county status concerns the town's civic jurisdiction rather than a hereditary earldom.

titles.name: Honour of Skipton
titles.note: The local honour and Clifford lordship are attested. Forfeitures and restoration during the 1460s and Readeption require a specific early-1471 tenure audit; neither Stanley possession in configuration nor geographical Yorkshire establishes a Duchy of York parent.
titles.description: Honour of Skipton is centred on Skipton Castle. It is associated with Craven, West Riding of Yorkshire. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Lordship of Middleham
titles.note: The Neville inheritance and local lordship are established. Earlier origin in Alan Rufus's lands is not sufficient proof of continuing 1471 mesne dependence on Richmond. Warwick/Salisbury ownership likewise does not make their remote dignity the territorial parent. Exclude the subsequent Gloucester settlement.
titles.description: Lordship of Middleham is centred on Middleham Castle. It is associated with Wensleydale, North Riding of Yorkshire.

titles.name: Honour of Richmond
titles.area: Richmondshire, North Riding of Yorkshire; dispersed honour estates
titles.note: Castle and honour were surrendered to the Crown in 1372. Edward IV granted lands and castle to Clarence in 1462 expressly without the earldom. Crown superiority is proposed from this grant history, pending Readeption confirmation. Do not identify honour, earldom dignity and Clarence's possession as one thing.
titles.description: Honour of Richmond is centred on Richmond Castle. It is associated with Richmondshire, North Riding of Yorkshire; dispersed honour estates. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Lordship of Helmsley
titles.note: The official guide identifies Helmsley's manorial administrative role and the de Ros family castle. This supports a local estate, not automatic Duchy of York superiority. The Ros forfeiture, dower and 1471 reversion interests require more precise legal evidence before assigning a parent or changing ownership.
titles.description: Lordship of Helmsley is centred on Helmsley Castle. It is associated with Ryedale, North Riding of Yorkshire.

titles.name: Borough of Kingston upon Hull
titles.area: East Riding of Yorkshire; Hullshire from 1440/1447
titles.note: Royal borough created in 1299; Hull History Centre records county status in 1440 and extension in 1447, confirmed by Edward IV in 1462. This municipal county is not a comital dignity or a Duchy of York subdivision.
titles.description: Borough of Kingston upon Hull is centred on Kingston upon Hull. It is associated with East Riding of Yorkshire; Hullshire from 1440/1447. Its county status concerns the town's civic jurisdiction rather than a hereditary earldom.

titles.name: Scarborough castle estate
titles.note: Official history identifies the major royal castle. Direct Crown parent is proposed from this documented institutional status pending the particular early-1471 custody/grant instrument. A constable's family title does not turn it into a private barony, and Hull's civic jurisdiction is not its territorial parent.
titles.description: Scarborough castle estate is centred on Scarborough Castle. It is associated with North Riding of Yorkshire.

titles.name: Lordship of Hallamshire
titles.note: Sheffield lay within the historic Hallamshire lordship, later the Furnival/Talbot inheritance. Neither the Talbots' Shrewsbury dignity nor Yorkshire location establishes superior territorial tenure. Keep the local lordship and leave its immediate superior unresolved.
titles.description: Lordship of Hallamshire is centred on Sheffield. It is associated with West Riding of Yorkshire.

titles.name: Honour of Conisbrough
titles.note: English Heritage explicitly identifies the Warenne honour and its later House of York association. It was a separate estate from neighbouring Hallamshire. A shared York holder does not establish legal subordination to the titular duchy; the exact early-1471 superior remains unverified.
titles.description: Honour of Conisbrough is centred on Conisbrough Castle. It is associated with West Riding of Yorkshire. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Nottingham castle estate
titles.note: The archaeological report states that Nottingham remained a royal castle until its effective sale in 1622. It is not geographically within Hallamshire; a Hastings constableship or configured owner does not create a feudal Hallamshire parent.
titles.description: Nottingham castle estate is centred on Nottingham Castle. It is associated with Nottinghamshire.

titles.name: City of Lincoln

holder.hero_name: John de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk

possessor.hero_name: John de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk

titles.area: Lincolnshire; county of the city from 1409
titles.note: The royal charter series and council account establish civic county status from 1409. Direct royal civic relationship is proposed; medieval fee-farm and exempt ecclesiastical properties still require examination. The Earl of Lincoln's dignity does not convey the city or shire wholesale.
titles.description: City of Lincoln is centred on Lincoln. It is associated with Lincolnshire; county of the city from 1409. Its county status concerns the town's civic jurisdiction rather than a hereditary earldom.

titles.name: Lordship of Tattershall
titles.note: A local fortified manor/lordship inherited by Ralph Cromwell, then Joan and Humphrey Bourchier before Humphrey's death in 1471. The source does not identify an immediate mesne lord. Later Crown acquisition and the Clinton Earls of Lincoln are excluded from the early-spring mapping.
titles.description: Lordship of Tattershall is centred on Tattershall Castle. It is associated with Lindsey, Lincolnshire.

titles.name: Stafford castle estate
titles.note: The official history connects the castle to the Stafford inheritance and the creation of the Buckingham dukedom in 1444. Local estate is a conservative descriptive label pending the barony's tenure record. Shared ownership does not prove a geographical duchy of Buckingham covering surrounding shires.
titles.description: Stafford castle estate is centred on Stafford Castle. It is associated with Staffordshire. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: City of Hereford
titles.note: The city has its own royal charter history. Neither the Hereford earldom nor the Bergavenny dignity proves title to the city. Retain its actual local civic identity; a precise medieval fee-farm/tenure instrument is needed before assigning an immediate superior.
titles.description: City of Hereford is centred on Hereford. It is associated with Herefordshire.

titles.name: Lordship of Brecknock
titles.note: Powys Archives identifies the lordship's passage by inheritance to Buckingham in the fifteenth century; Coflein confirms the castle and borough are distinct. Brecknock is the territorial identity, not Herefordshire or Bergavenny. Buckingham's possession alone does not establish an intermediate superior dignity.
titles.description: Lordship of Brecknock is centred on Brecon Castle. It is associated with Brecknock, Welsh March. A Marcher lordship combines landed authority with the distinctive rights and customs of the Welsh March.

titles.name: Lordship of Painscastle
titles.area: Elfael Is Mynydd, Welsh March (later Radnorshire)
titles.note: RCAHMW identifies the castle as the administrative centre of a lordship encompassing Elfael Is Mynydd in the twelfth century. Persistence and exact 1471 superior tenure require later grants or inquisitions; the local identity is a proposed historical continuity, not proof of Grey of Wilton ownership or Hereford superiority.
titles.description: Lordship of Painscastle is centred on Painscastle. It is associated with Elfael Is Mynydd, Welsh March (later Radnorshire). A Marcher lordship combines landed authority with the distinctive rights and customs of the Welsh March.

titles.name: Borough of Shrewsbury
titles.note: The council records a royal charter sequence beginning before John's surviving 1199 charter. Crown parent is proposed for the civic jurisdiction pending medieval fee-farm and franchise detail. The Talbot earldom does not imply ownership of the borough or superior tenure over every Shropshire castle.
titles.description: Borough of Shrewsbury is centred on Shrewsbury. It is associated with Shropshire.

titles.name: Lordship of Ludlow
titles.note: The Lacy/Geneville/Mortimer estate passed to Richard of York in 1425 and became royal with Edward IV. Its historical relation to Stanton Lacy and earlier Montgomery tenure does not prove continuing 1471 subordination. Do not parent it to Talbot's Earldom of Shrewsbury from its shire location.
titles.description: Lordship of Ludlow is centred on Ludlow Castle. It is associated with Shropshire, Welsh March.

titles.name: Lordship of Montgomery
titles.note: Cadw establishes the royal foundation; the later Mortimer estate history cautions against assuming unchanged direct Crown possession. Local Marcher lordship is the proposed territorial unit. Precise early-1471 superior tenure needs confirmation; neither Grey of Codnor nor Shrewsbury follows from configuration.
titles.description: Lordship of Montgomery is centred on Montgomery Castle. It is associated with Montgomery, Welsh March. A Marcher lordship combines landed authority with the distinctive rights and customs of the Welsh March.

titles.name: Lordship of Framlingham

holder.hero_name: John de Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk

possessor.hero_name: John de Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk

titles.note: Local manor and castle, subsequently a Mowbray estate, are evidenced. Association with the dukes of Norfolk does not establish a territorial duchy covering Suffolk or subordinate every neighbouring estate; the 1471 superior tenure needs an inquisition or grant.
titles.description: Lordship of Framlingham is centred on Framlingham Castle. It is associated with Suffolk.

titles.name: City and County of Norwich
titles.note: Royal charter made Norwich a county corporate in 1404. This is civic jurisdiction under the Crown, not an earldom and not evidence of subordination to the duke of Norfolk.
titles.description: City and County of Norwich is centred on Norwich. It is associated with Norfolk. Its county status concerns the town's civic jurisdiction rather than a hereditary earldom.

titles.name: Manor of Baconsthorpe
titles.note: Heydon manor and castle, built from the mid fifteenth century. John Heydon's service to the duke of Suffolk was affinity, not demonstrated feudal subordination. A parliamentary Barony of Baconsthorpe and a Norwich-earldom parent are not established.
titles.description: Manor of Baconsthorpe is centred on Baconsthorpe Castle. It is associated with Norfolk. The manor is a local estate whose lands and customary rights form a distinct lordship.

titles.name: Borough of Lynn Episcopi

holder.hero_name: John de Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk

possessor.hero_name: John de Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk

titles.historical_superior: Temporalities of the Bishopric of Norwich
titles.note: The bishop was a borough lord until the sixteenth century; the town leased substantial jurisdiction and the lord of Rising also had rights. This is a simplified episcopal superior candidate, not an exclusive assertion over every burgage. Record for church branch; retain current game owner.
titles.description: Borough of Lynn Episcopi is centred on Lynn. It is associated with Norfolk.

titles.name: Liberty of St Edmund

holder.hero_name: John de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk

possessor.hero_name: John de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk

titles.note: The abbey's major local authority supports an abbatial borough/liberty model, not the duke of Suffolk's territorial earldom. Exact liberty boundary and exemptions require charter work; this source is institutional history rather than a 1471 extent. Church branch follow-up; no ownership change.
titles.description: Liberty of St Edmund is centred on Bury St. Edmunds. It is associated with Suffolk.

titles.name: Honour of Clare
titles.note: Clare was the head of a genuine honour with dispersed estates. Its inheritance is distinct from a generic County of Suffolk. The legal superior and the effect of Yorkist grants/readeption in early 1471 are not established here; no Norfolk/Suffolk peerage parent is inferred.
titles.description: Honour of Clare is centred on Clare Castle. It is associated with Suffolk. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Borough of Colchester
titles.note: Royal-chartered borough beside a royal castle; no evidence that the Bourchier earldom of Essex conferred lordship of the town. Borough liberties and the castle estate must be distinguished. Crown relationship is a civic candidate pending the borough fee-farm/charter extent.
titles.description: Borough of Colchester is centred on Colchester. It is associated with Essex.

titles.name: Lordship of Castle Hedingham

holder.hero_name: John de Vere, Earl of Oxford

possessor.hero_name: John de Vere, Earl of Oxford

titles.note: De Vere castle and estate, associated with the earls of Oxford. Essex is the geographical shire, not a demonstrated Bourchier superior; the earldom of Oxford dignity alone does not establish an upper territorial estate.
titles.description: Lordship of Castle Hedingham is centred on Hedingham Castle. It is associated with Essex.

titles.name: Royal castle and manor of Corfe
titles.note: Royal castle until its sale in 1572. A constable's custody or the Somerset dignity does not convert it into the territorial Duchy of Somerset.
titles.description: Royal castle and manor of Corfe is centred on Corfe Castle. It is associated with Dorset; Isle of Purbeck.

titles.name: Town and County of Bristol
titles.note: The 1373 royal charter created civic county status. There was no corresponding earl of Bristol in 1471. The charter does not make Chepstow, Gloucester, Farleigh, Wardour or Sherborne dependent baronies; Holland's remote Exeter dignity establishes no such hierarchy.
titles.description: Bristol received county status by royal charter in 1373. Its civic jurisdiction belonged to the town and was distinct from a hereditary earldom: the Town and County of Bristol did not require an Earl of Bristol.

titles.name: Lordship of Chepstow (Striguil)
titles.note: A separate marcher lordship, not a Bristol county dependency. Cadw supports local castle identity; the archive catalogues lordship records. These do not establish the precise 1471 superior tenure; neither Norfolk nor Somerset is inferred from a titleholder.
titles.description: Lordship of Chepstow (Striguil) is centred on Chepstow Castle. It is associated with Welsh March; lower Wye. A Marcher lordship combines landed authority with the distinctive rights and customs of the Welsh March.

titles.name: Royal castle of Gloucester
titles.note: Council conservation assessment describes Crown retention after hereditary sheriffs and later royal dower grants; castle also served the county gaol. Crown estate is the candidate, subject to a specific 1471 grant check. Neither Bristol civic county nor the Gloucester dignity alone supplies its territorial superior.
titles.description: Royal castle of Gloucester is centred on Gloucester Castle. It is associated with Gloucestershire.

titles.name: Manor of Farleigh Hungerford
titles.note: Local Hungerford manor and castle, confiscated after Yorkist victory in 1462 and restored in 1486. The Crown's confiscation and temporary custody do not establish a permanent Bristol or Somerset-duchy hierarchy. Early 1471 legal tenure remains to be checked.
titles.description: Manor of Farleigh Hungerford is centred on Farleigh Castle. It is associated with Somerset. The manor is a local estate whose lands and customary rights form a distinct lordship.

titles.name: Episcopal estate of Sherborne
titles.historical_superior: Temporalities of the Bishopric of Salisbury
titles.note: Bishop Wyvill recovered the castle in 1354; it then served the bishopric's administration and residence. Not an estate of Exeter merely because Holland holds it in the mod. Document for church branch; do not alter current ownership here.
titles.description: Episcopal estate of Sherborne is centred on Sherborne Castle. It is associated with Dorset. The estate's history is tied to the temporal lands of a bishopric.

titles.name: Manor of Wardour
titles.note: Lovell manor and castle forfeited in 1461; source records subsequent changing ownership. Exact effects of the 1470 readeption require grant evidence. Neither Bristol nor the Somerset dignity is a demonstrated superior.
titles.description: Manor of Wardour is centred on Wardour Castle. It is associated with Wiltshire. The manor is a local estate whose lands and customary rights form a distinct lordship.

titles.name: City of Exeter
titles.note: Civic territory with royal charters, not automatically the earldom of Devon or Holland's duchy of Exeter. Charter-calendar transcription supports royal liberties; fee-farm extent remains to be verified. Distinguish the city, Rougemont castle, cathedral close and Courtenay estates; county-corporate status dates only to 1537.
titles.description: City of Exeter is centred on Exeter. It is associated with Devon.

titles.name: Honour of Dunster
titles.note: A local Mohun/Luttrell honour, affected by Yorkist forfeiture and Herbert grants. This establishes no Devon-earldom or Somerset-duchy superior. Need the relevant grant/inquisition to resolve superior tenure and early 1471 reversals independently of control.
titles.description: Honour of Dunster is centred on Dunster Castle. It is associated with Somerset. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Borough of Plymouth
titles.note: 1439 incorporation and parliamentary royal licence for municipal fortification support a borough/civic castle rather than a noble Barony of Plymouth. They do not by themselves settle residual manorial superior rights; do not infer Courtenay or Blount homage from geography.
titles.description: Borough of Plymouth is centred on Plymouth Castle. It is associated with Devon.

titles.name: Barony of Totnes
titles.note: Castle estate descended through de Nonant, de Braose and Zouche. Local barony is the candidate, distinct from the separately privileged borough. The earldom of Devon is not established as superior; 1471 tenure and estate extent need documentary confirmation.
titles.description: Barony of Totnes is centred on Totnes Castle. It is associated with Devon.

titles.name: Manor of Taunton Deane
titles.historical_superior: Temporalities of the Bishopric of Winchester
titles.note: Taunton castle was the capital messuage of Winchester's manor of Taunton Deane. Not a Devon-earldom dependency. Church-branch documentation only; retain current game ownership.
titles.description: Manor of Taunton Deane is centred on Taunton Castle. It is associated with Somerset. The manor belongs to the historical pattern of episcopal landed estates.

titles.name: Honour of Launceston
titles.note: 1337 charter includes Launceston castle, borough, manor and honour in the duchy. This is a territorial estate connection, not an assumption that every Cornish estate belongs to the duke. Possession during rival royal successions is a separate question.
titles.description: Honour of Launceston is centred on Launceston. It is associated with Cornwall. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Barony of Okehampton
titles.note: The source explicitly identifies the barony inherited by Hugh Courtenay in 1292, before his family gained the Devon earldom. Okehampton is in Devon, not Cornwall. Courtenay ownership does not alone prove that this barony was legally held of the earldom; superior remains unverified.
titles.description: Barony of Okehampton is centred on Okehampton Castle. It is associated with Devon.

titles.name: Priory estate of St Michael's Mount
titles.note: Alien priory appropriated under Henry V and Mount lands transferred to Syon, confirmed in 1424. Castle occupation or military custody must be separate from monastic title. Record for church branch; no ownership change in this artifact.
titles.description: Priory estate of St Michael's Mount is centred on St. Michael's Mount Castle. It is associated with Cornwall. The estate's history is tied to the landed possessions of a religious house.

titles.name: Royal castle and borough of Harlech
titles.note: Edwardian royal castle, not the caput of a duchy covering all Wales. Principality territory is the candidate; the relevant late-medieval annexation/grants and local extent need confirmation. Its 1468 capture changes control, not the territorial identity.
titles.description: Royal castle and borough of Harlech is centred on Harlech Castle. It is associated with Merioneth; Gwynedd.

titles.name: Castle and borough of Cardiff
titles.note: Cardiff is the castle/borough of the Glamorgan marcher lordship. The local territorial connection is supported by the castle history; it should not be nested in the royal Principality of Wales merely because both are Welsh. Titleholder and rival claims in 1471 remain separate.
titles.description: Castle and borough of Cardiff is centred on Cardiff. It is associated with Glamorgan; Welsh March.

titles.name: Castle and borough of Swansea
titles.note: Archaeological reports identify Swansea as the administrative seat of the marcher lordship of Gower. This is not a Glamorgan or Principality dependency simply because of a modern county boundary or common owner.
titles.description: Castle and borough of Swansea is centred on Swansea Castle. It is associated with Gower; Welsh March.

titles.name: Castle estate of Caerphilly
titles.note: De Clare castle in the Glamorgan complex; Glamorgan superior is a candidate pending an extent establishing its exact local lordship and 1471 tenure. Do not derive it merely from the Warwick/Neville holder's distant dignity.
titles.description: Castle estate of Caerphilly is centred on Caerphilly Castle. It is associated with Senghenydd; Glamorgan; Welsh March. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Earldom of Pembroke
titles.note: A genuine local earldom incorporating the castle, unlike an invented county container; local castle trust records its regrant to Jasper Tudor. Precise palatine extent and superior legal wording need the charter. Do not make Carmarthen subordinate or equate this estate with all modern Pembrokeshire. Spring1471 claimant/control require separate dating.
titles.description: The Earldom of Pembroke is centred on Pembroke and its castle in south-west Wales. Its history is closely bound to the struggle between the houses of Lancaster and York, with rival Tudor and Herbert claims to the dignity.

titles.name: Royal castle of Carmarthen
titles.note: Cadw records Crown possession and its role as the royal administrative centre of south-west Wales. Candidate principality parent requires late-medieval grant verification; Pembroke's earl briefly recapturing the castle in 1223 does not establish a permanent Pembroke earldom dependency.
titles.description: Royal castle of Carmarthen is centred on Carmarthen Castle. It is associated with Carmarthenshire; south-west Wales.

titles.name: Royal castle and borough of Aberystwyth
titles.note: Royal Edwardian foundation; Ceredigion is geographical context, not a demonstrated 1471 earldom. Principality superior is provisional until the specific late-medieval royal estate/borough grants are checked.
titles.description: Royal castle and borough of Aberystwyth is centred on Aberystwyth. It is associated with Cardiganshire; Ceredigion.

titles.name: Castle estate of Cardigan
titles.note: Official monuments-board history establishes the castle's identity and Rhys ap Gruffudd's twelfth-century construction. This is a local descriptive estate pending documentary verification of royal title and 1471 grants; no County of Ceredigion peerage or Aberystwyth superior is asserted.
titles.description: Castle estate of Cardigan is centred on Cardigan Castle. It is associated with Cardiganshire; Ceredigion. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Royal castle and borough of Caernarfon
titles.note: Royal Edwardian castle and borough. Principality parent is a candidate requiring late-medieval estate/grant verification. A generic County of Gwynedd is not an earldom and should not imply homage to a local earl.
titles.description: Royal castle and borough of Caernarfon is centred on Caernarfon. It is associated with Caernarfonshire; Gwynedd.

titles.name: Royal castle and borough of Conwy
titles.note: Royal Edwardian foundation. Principality parent is provisional pending the relevant fifteenth-century estate grants; modern/historical geographic Gwynedd is not itself proof of a count's jurisdiction.
titles.description: Royal castle and borough of Conwy is centred on Conwy Castle. It is associated with Caernarfonshire; Gwynedd.

titles.name: Royal castle and borough of Beaumaris
titles.note: Cadw explicitly identifies Edward I's royal stronghold. Principality is a proposed superior pending a precise 1471 grant/estate check, rather than a fabricated Gwynedd earldom.
titles.description: Royal castle and borough of Beaumaris is centred on Beaumaris Castle. It is associated with Anglesey; Gwynedd.

titles.name: Lordship of Denbigh
titles.note: A local marcher lordship founded for Henry de Lacy, rather than a barony subordinate to an invented Gwynedd county. Crown/York/Lancaster grants and the 1470 readeption require separate legal checking. Denbigh identity must stay anchored here, never transferred to Pembroke because the owner shares another title.
titles.description: Lordship of Denbigh is centred on Denbigh Castle. It is associated with Perfeddwlad; north-east Welsh March. A Marcher lordship combines landed authority with the distinctive rights and customs of the Welsh March.

titles.name: City of London
titles.note: Royal charters confirmed civic liberties and self-government. This is municipal jurisdiction, not a noble County of London. Westminster and ecclesiastical estates are distinct and must not inherit City's liberties merely through a game village binding.
titles.description: City of London is centred on London. It is associated with London; Middlesex.

titles.name: Royal castle estate of Windsor
titles.note: Royal castle and residence. Historic England distinguishes the underlying leased Clewer land, purchased only in 1546: map castle jurisdiction without claiming every nearby manor was Crown freehold. Not a City of London dependency.
titles.description: Royal castle estate of Windsor is centred on Windsor Castle. It is associated with Berkshire.

titles.name: Honour of Berkhamsted
titles.note: A real dispersed honour incorporated into the Duchy of Cornwall in 1337; this demonstrates why territorial estate membership cannot be inferred from shire or proximity. Later queens' residence and custody are separate from the honour's legal identity.
titles.description: Honour of Berkhamsted is centred on Berkhamsted Castle. It is associated with Hertfordshire. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Castle estate of Hertford
titles.note: Royal palace, granted to John of Gaunt in 1360 and regained by Henry IV after 1399; Edward IV rebuilt the gatehouse in 1463-65. Need title deeds to distinguish Duchy of Lancaster estate from other Crown demesne under the rival 1471 regimes. Neither is replaced with a fictional London county parent.
titles.description: Castle estate of Hertford is centred on Hertford Castle. It is associated with Hertfordshire.

titles.name: City and County of Canterbury
titles.note: 1448 civic charter and 1461 county status establish the municipal entity, not Grey's earldom of Kent. Cathedral, archiepiscopal and monastic liberties are separate and must not be absorbed wholesale by a town polygon.
titles.description: City and County of Canterbury is centred on Canterbury. It is associated with Kent. Its county status concerns the town's civic jurisdiction rather than a hereditary earldom.

titles.name: Royal castle of Dover

holder.hero_name: Richard West, Lord De La Warr

possessor.hero_name: Richard West, Lord De La Warr

titles.note: Royal fortress and residence, remodelled by Edward IV. Constableship and wardenship of the Cinque Ports are offices, not proof of a hereditary barony held of the earl of Kent.
titles.description: Royal castle of Dover is centred on Dover Castle. It is associated with Kent; Cinque Ports.

titles.name: Castle estate of Rochester
titles.note: Local castle distinct from the bishop's palace and cathedral. Its history involves Crown and archbishop, so the precise fifteenth-century superior needs grant evidence. No Kent-earldom dependency is inferred from geographical location.
titles.description: Castle estate of Rochester is centred on Rochester Castle. It is associated with Kent. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Castle and Lowy of Tonbridge
titles.historical_superior: Temporalities of the Archbishopric of Canterbury
titles.note: A genuine castle/lowy and de Clare-Stafford estate, not generic Kent-earldom land. Medieval inquisition and scholarly history support archiepiscopal homage/rights; carry-forward to 1471 is provisional pending the Buckingham inquisition. Do not confuse Crown wardship with cancellation of Canterbury's superior rights.
titles.description: Castle and Lowy of Tonbridge is centred on Tonbridge Castle. It is associated with Kent; lowy extending into Surrey. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Antient Town of Rye
titles.note: Rye's Cinque Ports privileges are a civic/service relationship with the Crown, not a Grey barony or earldom of Kent estate. Precise 1471 land-tenure and castle custody need checking separately; geographical area is Sussex.
titles.description: Antient Town of Rye is centred on Rye Castle. It is associated with Sussex; Cinque Ports.

titles.name: City of Chichester
titles.note: Royal-chartered civic body and distinct local tenements are evidenced. A city-wide Fitzalan overlordship cannot be inferred from the earldom of Arundel or an administrative County of Sussex; borough, cathedral liberty and rape require separate tenure work.
titles.description: City of Chichester is centred on Chichester. It is associated with Sussex; rape of Chichester.

titles.name: Barony and honour of Lewes
titles.note: Castle administered the Warenne territorial holdings of the rape; later earls of Arundel held it. Local honour remains distinct from the Arundel honour and the Surrey dignity. Upper legal tenure in 1471 remains unverified.
titles.description: Barony and honour of Lewes is centred on Lewes Castle. It is associated with Sussex; rape of Lewes. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Honour of Arundel
titles.note: Castle and honour demonstrably linked to the earldom and inherited by Fitzalans. This does not make the entire Sussex shire a single county estate or subsume Lewes/Chichester. No intermediate superior is asserted without tenure evidence.
titles.description: Honour of Arundel is centred on Arundel Castle. It is associated with Sussex; rape of Arundel. An honour brings together estates and rights under a common lordship; its lands need not form a single continuous territory.

titles.name: Town and County of Southampton
titles.note: Henry VI's 1447 charter made the town a county with its own sheriff. This is civic county status, not an earldom encompassing Hampshire's castles or a territorial possession automatically attached to Stafford.
titles.description: Town and County of Southampton is centred on Southampton. It is associated with Hampshire. Its county status concerns the town's civic jurisdiction rather than a hereditary earldom.

titles.name: Lordship of the Isle of Wight
titles.note: Carisbrooke was the island's central castle; the Crown acquired it in 1293 but grants and governorships changed subsequently. Exact 1471 royal/ Woodville/ Lancastrian grants must be checked before asserting a superior. Southampton's civic county supplies no island overlordship.
titles.description: Lordship of the Isle of Wight is centred on Carisbrooke Castle. It is associated with Isle of Wight; Hampshire.

titles.name: Episcopal manor of Farnham
titles.historical_superior: Temporalities of the Bishopric of Winchester
titles.note: Farnham lands and castle belonged to the bishops of Winchester. Surrey location and episcopal estate identity are distinct from Hampshire or Southampton civic county. Church branch documentation; do not change current game owner.
titles.description: Episcopal manor of Farnham is centred on Farnham Castle. It is associated with Surrey. The manor belongs to the historical pattern of episcopal landed estates.

titles.name: Royal castle of Winchester
titles.note: Royal castle, hall and gaol; distinguish it from the bishop's Wolvesey Palace. Southampton's civic county does not extend over Winchester. A custodian or current game owner is not automatically the holder of a territorial Hampshire dignity.
titles.description: Royal castle of Winchester is centred on Winchester Castle. It is associated with Hampshire.

titles.name: Borough of Oxford

holder.hero_name: John de Vere, Earl of Oxford

possessor.hero_name: John de Vere, Earl of Oxford

titles.note: Civic commune and 1199 fee-farm support a royal-borough candidate. De Vere's Oxford earldom did not by its name make the borough or entire shire his territorial demesne. Castle, university liberties and borough need separate extents; municipal superior should be verified against the fee-farm charter.
titles.description: Borough of Oxford is centred on Oxford. It is associated with Oxfordshire; south-bank suburbs historically Berkshire.

titles.name: Manor of Donnington

holder.hero_name: John de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk

possessor.hero_name: John de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk

titles.note: Abberbury manor purchased by Thomas Chaucer and inherited into the de la Pole family. Not in Oxfordshire and not an Oxford-earldom dependency; the family's Suffolk dignity is also not a substitute for local superior tenure. The manor's exact 1471 tenure remains unverified.
titles.description: Manor of Donnington is centred on Donnington Castle. It is associated with Berkshire. The manor is a local estate whose lands and customary rights form a distinct lordship.

titles.name: Lordship of Warkworth
titles.note: The castle and manor formed a local estate granted to the Percys in 1332. Their inheritance and earldom restoration in 1470–71 requires care in a precise start-date audit. Percy ownership does not mean the territorial earldom has superior tenure over every Northumberland estate; no such parent is asserted.
titles.description: Lordship of Warkworth is centred on Warkworth. It is associated with Northumberland.

titles.name: Bamburgh castle estate
titles.note: The research account identifies Crown ownership until the Union of the Crowns; the council appraisal records Wars of the Roses fighting. Direct Crown parent is proposed from institutional status, pending a 1471 grant/custody audit. Lumley garrison/ownership configuration does not prove a private barony under Percy.
titles.description: Bamburgh castle estate is centred on Bamburgh Castle. It is associated with Northumberland.

titles.name: Dunstanburgh castle estate
titles.note: Founded by Thomas of Lancaster and developed by John of Gaunt; it remained a Lancastrian estate and stronghold. Duchy parent is proposed from that estate history, pending the exact early-1471 tenure account. Location within Northumberland does not subordinate it to the Percy earldom.
titles.description: Dunstanburgh castle estate is centred on Dunstanburgh Castle. It is associated with Northumberland. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Edinburgh

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

possessor.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: Royal charter dated 1124 x 1127. The burgh is a separate jurisdiction; Lothian is a historical region, not evidence for an earldom over Edinburgh. Surrounding rural estates require their own tenure evidence.
titles.description: Royal burgh of Edinburgh is centred on Edinburgh. It is associated with Lothian; Edinburgh sheriffdom. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Burgh and royal fortress of Berwick

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

possessor.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: Town and castle passed to Scotland in 1461 and remained Scottish until 1482. This supports Scottish royal administration in 1471, not a restored Earl of March's territorial lordship. The detailed burgh tenure and privileges in this interval remain to be checked.
titles.description: Burgh and royal fortress of Berwick is centred on Berwick-upon-Tweed. It is associated with Berwick; East March. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Dunbar castle estate

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

possessor.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: Descriptive local estate pending a 1471 castle charter. Dunbar burgh became royal in 1445, but this inventory seat is the castle. Neither the burgh's status nor the historical earldom proves this castle's immediate superior in 1471.
titles.description: Dunbar castle estate is centred on Dunbar. It is associated with East Lothian; Haddington sheriffdom. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Stirling
titles.note: Stirling Archives dates the royal burgh's creation to 1124 x 1127. A keeper or noble with royal service does not turn the burgh into that family's hereditary lordship. Royal castle and rural lands should be distinguished from the burgh franchise.
titles.description: Royal burgh of Stirling is centred on Stirling. It is associated with Stirling sheriffdom. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Regality of Glasgow
titles.note: Glasgow was the bishop's burgh, raised to a regality in 1450. The local episcopal jurisdiction should not be labelled Hamilton merely because of the current clan owner or geography. Record for the church branch; this research does not change ownership.
titles.description: Regality of Glasgow is centred on Glasgow. It is associated with Clydesdale; Lanark sheriffdom. The estate's history is tied to the temporal lands of a bishopric.

titles.name: Royal castle of Rothesay
titles.note: The Stewart family castle became royal when the Stewarts became kings in 1371. Royal identity is established; the 1471 estate's relationship to the heir's Duchy of Rothesay requires the relevant endowment to be checked. No territorial link to Hamilton or Lanark is established here.
titles.description: Royal castle of Rothesay is centred on Rothesay Castle. It is associated with Bute. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Ayr
titles.note: The council's historical account identifies the royal burgh charter of 1205. Ayr itself is in Kyle: neither Kennedy's possession in the game nor the royal dignity of Carrick establishes a Kennedy lordship over the burgh. Rural Kennedy lands need separate mapping.
titles.description: Royal burgh of Ayr is centred on Ayr. It is associated with Kyle; Ayr sheriffdom. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Dumfries
titles.note: Museum catalogue of the surviving charter copy identifies the royal foundation of 1186. Dumfries burgh is distinct from Maxwell's Caerlaverock estate and from the wider Nithsdale region. Do not manufacture an Earldom of Dumfries from the number of settlements currently owned together.
titles.description: Dumfries is a royal burgh founded in 1186. Its burgh jurisdiction is distinct from the surrounding region of Nithsdale and from the Maxwell estate at Caerlaverock. The burgh's status rests on its royal foundation rather than an earldom of Dumfries.

titles.name: Lands of Caerlaverock
titles.note: The estate account records AlexanderII's 1220 grant of Caerlaverock lands to John Maxwell. This supports a distinct local Maxwell estate; its complete 1471 legal description and continuing immediate superiority need charter verification. The name Lord Maxwell is a dignity, not a reason to absorb Dumfries burgh.
titles.description: Lands of Caerlaverock is centred on Caerlaverock. It is associated with Nithsdale; Dumfries sheriffdom. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Threave castle estate

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

possessor.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: HES identifies Threave as the Douglas seat of the lordship of Galloway and records castle and lordship annexed to the Crown in 1455. Map the local estate under that territorial lordship, with royal possession separate. It is not a dependency of Caerlaverock merely because the game gives both to Maxwell.
titles.description: Threave castle estate is centred on Threave. It is associated with Galloway; Kirkcudbright stewartry. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Hermitage castle estate
titles.note: HES explicitly associates Hermitage with the lordship of Liddesdale and Douglas tenure before 1491. An owner holding the Angus dignity does not move Hermitage into the territorial earldom of Angus; Nithsdale is also the wrong geographical container.
titles.description: Hermitage stands in Liddesdale in the Scottish Borders. Its castle and surrounding estate are associated with the lordship of Liddesdale and the Douglas family. The estate has its own territorial identity, distinct from the Earldom of Angus held by its Douglas lords.

titles.name: Episcopal burgh of St Andrews

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: University archive records the bishop's foundation between 1124 and 1144; full royal-burgh status came in 1620. Use Bishopric, not Archbishopric, for early 1471: metropolitan promotion followed in 1472. Church household implementation and the existing ownership placeholder remain deferred to the church branch as requested.
titles.description: Episcopal burgh of St Andrews is centred on Saint Andrews. It is associated with Fife. The estate's history is tied to the temporal lands of a bishopric.

titles.name: Lochleven castle estate
titles.note: HES records RobertII's grant of the previously royal castle to Henry Douglas. That is evidence for a distinct Douglas castle estate, not for subordination to an Earl of Fife. Exact 1471 tenure and whether the royal grant retained direct superiority remain to be verified.
titles.description: Lochleven castle estate is centred on Lochleven. It is associated with Kinross; Fife region. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Dundee
titles.note: The council's charter account traces royal rights to William the Lion and RobertI's confirmation of 1327. This supports a royal burgh separate from the Crawford dignity. Crawford's local offices, influence or other estates do not turn all Dundee land into earldom demesne.
titles.description: Royal burgh of Dundee is centred on Dundee. It is associated with Angus; Forfar sheriffdom. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Perth
titles.note: Council history cites royal charters of DavidI, WilliamI in 1210 and RobertI in 1314. Perth burgh is not the same legal entity as Ruthven's nearby estates. Gowrie can be retained as historical geography, without inventing a 1471 earldom or Ruthven superiority over the burgh.
titles.description: Royal burgh of Perth is centred on Perth. It is associated with Gowrie; Perth sheriffdom. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Kilchurn castle estate
titles.note: HES identifies Kilchurn as Sir Colin Campbell of Glenorchy's mid-fifteenth-century base. Glenorchy is the proposed local estate group; the defining charter and its superior are still required. Shared Campbell ancestry does not itself establish the Earl of Argyll's immediate superiority.
titles.description: Kilchurn castle estate is centred on Kilchurn Castle. It is associated with Glenorchy; Lochawe; Argyll. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Aberdeen
titles.note: The council's historical account identifies royal-burgh status before 1150 and William the Lion's charter to the king's burgesses. Aberdeen's burgh is distinct from Keith estates or the Marischal dignity. This row concerns New Aberdeen; episcopal Old Aberdeen requires separate church treatment if represented.
titles.description: Royal burgh of Aberdeen is centred on Aberdeen. It is associated with Aberdeen sheriffdom. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Dunnottar castle estate
titles.note: Local Keith stronghold documented by the historic-environment record and castle history. This does not establish that an Earldom Marischal formed a territorial intermediate superior over the estate in 1471. Use the descriptive estate pending charter evidence; do not attach it to Aberdeen burgh.
titles.description: Dunnottar castle estate is centred on Dunnottar. It is associated with Mearns; Kincardine sheriffdom. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Kildrummy castle estate

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

possessor.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: HES identifies the castle as the seat of the earls of Mar. The territorial identity persists through fifteenth-century disputes and royal control; it is not Marischal or Aberdeen burgh. This row establishes the estate's territorial association, not the validity of any particular 1471 claimant.
titles.description: Kildrummy castle estate is centred on Kildrummy. It is associated with Mar; Aberdeen sheriffdom. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Elgin

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

possessor.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: The archaeological research framework dates royal-burgh status to 1130 x 1153. Moray is the region; Elgin burgh, cathedral property and the territorial earldom must be kept distinct. A current Earl of Moray's ownership of a game town is not evidence that the burgh is earldom demesne.
titles.description: Royal burgh of Elgin is centred on Elgin. It is associated with Moray; Elgin sheriffdom. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Lordship of Strathbogie
titles.note: The archaeological account identifies the former Strathbogie stronghold and RobertI's grant to Adam Gordon. Retain the local Strathbogie identity. Neither geographical proximity to Moray nor the holder's Huntly dignity proves a separate intermediate territorial superior; the 1471 charter chain requires verification.
titles.description: Lordship of Strathbogie is centred on Huntly. It is associated with Strathbogie; Aberdeen sheriffdom.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Inverness
titles.note: The scholarly burgh study identifies Inverness as a royal foundation of DavidI. Westfield is a separate estate, not the geographical title of the burgh. Sheriffship or family influence should be represented independently of the burgh's royal franchise.
titles.description: Royal burgh of Inverness is centred on Inverness. It is associated with Inverness sheriffdom; northern Moray. A royal burgh holds privileges granted by the Crown, giving the town a jurisdiction distinct from neighbouring landed estates.

titles.name: Lordship of Urquhart
titles.note: HES documents the medieval lordship, Crown reversion in 1346 and subsequent MacDonald control and conflict. These changes need a dated 1471 tenure check; possession, royal sovereignty and immediate superiority are not interchangeable. Do not backdate the Grant barony created in 1509 or automatically attach Urquhart to Ross.
titles.description: Lordship of Urquhart is centred on Urquhart Castle. It is associated with Glen Urquhart; Inverness sheriffdom.

titles.name: Thanage of Calder
titles.note: The Calder thanes and royal licence to fortify in 1454 support the local thanage identity. Direct Crown tenure is a candidate requiring the tenure charter: a fortification licence alone is not proof of immediate superiority. Avoid merging it into Inverness or importing later Campbell succession.
titles.description: Thanage of Calder is centred on Cawdor. It is associated with Nairn sheriffdom; Moray. A thanage is a Scottish territorial jurisdiction associated with the office and obligations of a thane.

titles.name: Town of Kirkwall

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

possessor.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: Kirkwall comprised earldom and ecclesiastical interests. Scottish royal-burgh charter is 1486. Sources date Sinclair's surrender to 1470 or 1471; precise effective date and local division need checking before assigning early-spring 1471 superiority. The 1468 pledge and 1472 parliamentary annexation are different events; do not backdate the latter.
titles.description: Town of Kirkwall is centred on Kirkwall. It is associated with Orkney Mainland.

titles.name: Wick settlement estate
titles.note: Descriptive local estate pending medieval town tenure. The castle source concerns nearby Old Wick, not proof that the represented town belonged to the same estate. Caithness geography does not establish this site's immediate feudal superior; Orkney is not a valid geographical parent merely through Sinclair title holdings.
titles.description: Wick settlement estate is centred on Wick. It is associated with Caithness.

titles.name: Dirlot castle estate

holder.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

possessor.hero_name: James III Stewart, King of Scots

titles.note: The council record identifies a fifteenth-century Sutherland family possession, followed by a royal grant to Odo/Y Makky in 1499. The later charter cannot simply be backdated. Exact 1471 tenure remains unresolved; neither Sinclair's Orkney earldom nor Sutherland kinship establishes an immediate superior.
titles.description: Dirlot castle estate is centred on Dirlot Castle. It is associated with Halkirk; Caithness. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Dornoch episcopal settlement
titles.note: Scholarly studies identify the cathedral and bishop's palace, with formal town burgh recognition only in 1628. Episcopal property is established, but the whole represented settlement's 1471 legal extent needs verification. Do not equate protection or kinship with the Earl of Sutherland to territorial superiority. Flag for the church branch without changing ownership.
titles.description: Dornoch episcopal settlement is centred on Dornoch. It is associated with Sutherland; diocese of Caithness. The estate's history is tied to the temporal lands of a bishopric.

titles.name: Finlaggan demesne
titles.note: Finlaggan was the lordship's residence, council and inauguration centre. Model its local demesne under the Lordship of the Isles, rather than invent a County of Islay. The lordship's relationship to the Scottish monarchy is distinct from the game's independent Isles faction root.
titles.description: Finlaggan demesne is centred on Finlaggan. It is associated with Islay.

titles.name: Dunyvaig castle estate
titles.note: The archaeological study places Dunyvaig in the MacDonald lordship's Islay context. Isles superiority is a 1471 candidate; the castle's contemporary charter and any intermediate local grant still need checking. Later MacDonald of Dunyvaig or Campbell arrangements must not be projected backward.
titles.description: Dunyvaig castle estate is centred on Dunyvaig. It is associated with Southern Islay. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Tarbert castle estate
titles.note: Recent archaeological scholarship revises assumptions about the castle's origins and royal association. Retain a local descriptive estate. Knapdale is relevant geography, but its lordship's general history is insufficient to settle this particular castle's immediate superior in 1471.
titles.description: Tarbert castle estate is centred on Tarbert Castle. It is associated with Tarbert; southern Knapdale; Kintyre isthmus. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Lands of Duart
titles.note: MacLean local estate; Isles superiority is provisional. SHS Acts notes Duart's later 1496 barony erection (A 50), not a 1471 barony.
titles.description: Lands of Duart is centred on Duart. It is associated with Torosay; Mull. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Stornoway settlement estate
titles.note: The official record says medieval castle origins are uncertain and its first historical reference is 1506; erection as the free barony of Lewis followed in 1511. Retain a descriptive local estate for the existing seat pending earlier tenure evidence. Do not backdate 1511, infer an Earldom of Lewis, or assume every MacLeod holding had identical superiority.
titles.description: Stornoway settlement estate is centred on Stornoway. It is associated with Lewis.

titles.name: Dunvegan castle estate
titles.note: HES establishes the medieval MacLeod seat and local castle history. This does not by itself prove the 1471 tenure chain. Dunvegan is on Skye, not Lewis; MacLeod's shared family name and service on an Isles council are not sufficient proof of immediate feudal superiority.
titles.description: Dunvegan castle estate is centred on Dunvegan. It is associated with Duirinish; Skye. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Lands of Barra
titles.note: SHS Acts no 21 records Alexander's 1427 grant of Barra to Gilleownan MacNeill, held from himself and heirs. Kisimul represents that local estate.
titles.description: Lands of Barra is centred on Kisimul. It is associated with Barra.

titles.name: Royal burgh of Dingwall
titles.note: The archaeological report dates the royal burgh to 1226 and separately identifies the castle as a principal seat of the earls of Ross. Burgh and earldom demesne must not be conflated. Royal foundation is verified, but 1471 burgh superiority and the polygon's rural extent need charter checking.
titles.description: Dingwall was established as a royal burgh in 1226. Its castle was a principal seat of the earls of Ross, but the burgh and the earldom's landed estate were distinct jurisdictions.

titles.name: Lands of Balnagown
titles.note: HES establishes the medieval Ross estate. The parish history transcribes a 1375 royal confirmation of the late Earl William's grant to Hugh Ross. Ross superiority is a candidate until that grant's tenure clause and 1471 continuation are checked. Avoid projecting a later formal barony backward.
titles.description: Lands of Balnagown is centred on Balnagowan. It is associated with Easter Ross; Kilmuir Easter. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Lands of Foulis
titles.note: The local Munro estate is established. The clan association reports a fourteenth-century charter from the Earl of Ross, supporting a candidate Ross relationship; this is a research lead until the actual charter and continued 1471 tenure are verified. No Crown or earldom link is inferred solely from geography.
titles.description: Lands of Foulis is centred on Foulis. It is associated with Kiltearn; Easter Ross. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Eilean Donan castle estate
titles.note: The archaeological research framework reports Richard Oram's evidence review: the earls of Ross developed and held the medieval castle, while Mackenzie involvement is unsupported before the later fifteenth century. Ross is a supported candidate, with exact 1471 tenure still unresolved; do not substitute a traditional early Mackenzie genealogy for documentary evidence.
titles.description: Eilean Donan castle estate is centred on Eilean Donan. It is associated with Kintail; Wester Ross. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Lands of Sleat
titles.note: SHS Acts no 96 documents John's 1469 grant to Hugh. Dunscaith's precise occupation date is less secure than Sleat's chartered tenure.
titles.description: Lands of Sleat is centred on Dunscaith. It is associated with Sleat; Skye.

titles.name: Inverlochy settlement estate
titles.note: SHS Acts A 9 records Lochaber's 1376 royal grant. Inverlochy's precise 1471 estate tenure still needs verification; Lochaber is not synonymous with Cameron's Lochiel.
titles.description: Inverlochy settlement estate is centred on Inverlochy. It is associated with Lochaber; Inverness sheriffdom.

titles.name: Tioram castle estate
titles.note: SHS Acts no 7 places Tioram within the Garmoran grant. Proposed grouping needs 1471 continuation checked; Moidart is distinct from Lochaber geography.
titles.description: Tioram castle estate is centred on Tioram. It is associated with Moidart; Garmoran. The castle forms the centre of a local landed estate.

titles.name: Lands of Ardnamurchan
titles.note: SHS Acts A 57's 1499 grant explicitly recalls service formerly owed to John, lord of Isles. Useful retrospective evidence;1471 continuity remains provisional.
titles.description: Lands of Ardnamurchan is centred on Mingary. It is associated with Ardnamurchan; Inverness sheriffdom.
